To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

children's adjustment to divorce is associated with (a) the absence of the noncustodial parent, (b) the quality of the custodial parent's relationship with the child, (c) parental conflict, (d) economic problems, and (e) the stressful life events associated with divorce and remarriage.

Children's adjustment to divorce is related to the quality of the custodial parent-child relationship, to the quality of relationships with both parents, and to the quality of their relationship with each other.

children's post-divorce adjustment is related to the quality of parenting provided by both parents, the quality of the relationship between the parents, and the quality and quantity of contact between the children and the parent who does not live with them.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how children adjust to divorce, how their adjustment can be understood in terms of the various perspectives that have been proposed, and how these perspectives are related.
the impact of divorce on children.
the effects of the divorce process on children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
children are more adversely affected by divorce if they experience a loss of parental care and/or parental conflict.

the child's adaptation to the divorce depends upon the child's perception of the divorce, the child's personality and temperament, the quality of the relationship with each parent, the quality of parenting, and the quality of relationships with the child's extended family.
the majority of children of divorce do adjust well and that a minority of children do not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the quality of the relationship between the child and the noncustodial parent is the single most important factor in the child's adaptation to divorce.

the quality of the relationship between the child and the non-residential parent, and the quality of the child's relationship with the resident parent and the child's relationship to the resident parent's partner, are the two most important predictors of children's adjustment following parental separation and divorce.
children of divorced families do not fare worse than children of married families.
The main takeaway from our work is that

children’s adjustment to their parents’ divorce depends on the quality of their relationship with each parent, the quality of their parents’ co-parenting relationship and their parents’ relationship with their ex-partners.
the effects of divorce on children are not uniform.
the effects of divorce on children’s adjustment are not as dire as many believe and that the effects are often temporary.
